newsitem.title: MALTA: Malta deposit banks see slower growth.
newsitem.headline: Malta deposit banks see slower growth.

text.p: The consolidated balance sheet of Malta's deposit money banks rose by 13.9 percent last year to reach 2,142.1 million Maltese pounds ($5,600.52 million) by the end of December, Malta Central Bank said.
In its 1996 annual report published late on Monday the bank said this compared to a growth rate of 19.3 percent in the previous year.
The Maltese banking system continued to be dominated by Mid-Med Bank and Bank of Valletta which accounted for well over 90 percent of domestic deposits and loans.

Loans and advances in 1996 rose by 141.2 million pounds, 15 percent, to 1,079.6 million pounds, with loans and advances to the private and parastatal sectors accounting for over half the banks' total asset portfolio. Local lending in 1995 had risen by 231 million pounds. .
Despite relatively weak demand for credit by the private and parastatal sectors, the banks' holdings of cash and deposits with the Central Bank dropped by 3.9 million pounds to 96.8 million pounds.

The banks' holding of local investments rose by 66.9 million (28.6 percent) to 301.3 million pounds as the banks bought an increasing number of Treasury bills, Malta government stock and other securities.
The banks' foreign assets rose by 26 million pounds, 4.7 percent, to 583.4 million, a slowdown from a 33.5 percent rise in 1995.

Resident deposits rose by 166.1 million (12.5 percent) to 1,496.5 million, slightly lower than the 12.8 percent growth in 1995. Savers showed an increased preference for time deposits following a 0.5 percent increase in interest rates in early 1996.

The Central Bank said residents' foreign currency deposits were up by by 9.6 percent to 160.5 million and foreign liabilities rose 18.7 percent to 229.6 million, a slowdown over 1995 as the banks made less use of sale and repurchase agreements with foreign banks.

The ratio of the banks' total liquid assets to their total deposit liabilities rose from 38.8 percent in December 1995 to 43.2 percent at the end of 1996 due to increased holding of Treasury bills and other marketable debt securities.
